# Where the returns came from

Long-term returns rarely come from a single dramatic decision. They accumulate from margins that widen slowly and capital that is reinvested without fuss.

## Margin before multiple

When we decompose a return, three things appear: earnings growth, the change in the valuation multiple, and distributions. Only the first compounds for long. The multiple can flatter a single year, but mean reversion takes the gain away again. That simple arithmetic shapes everything in this review, from how positions are sized to how long they are held. It is also why the discussion below spends so little time on what the market did in any one quarter.


:::quote
The multiple can flatter a year. Only earnings can flatter a decade.
:::

### What changed this year

Capital moved from cyclical names toward businesses with pricing power. The shift was gradual and is summarised in the table below.

Table: Sector weights at year end (illustrative).

| Sector | 2024 | 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Industrials | 24% | 21% | -3% |
| Software | 18% | 23% | 5% |
| Healthcare | 15% | 17% | 2% |
| Consumer | 22% | 19% | -3% |

# Risk, plainly stated

Risk is the chance of permanent loss, not the size of a monthly swing. We track it with a short list of questions rather than a single number, and we write the answers down before a purchase rather than after.

:::compare
##### What we watch

Debt maturities, customer concentration, and the honesty of the accounting.

---

##### What we ignore

Quarterly price targets, index membership changes, and next week's macro data.
:::

:::timeline
- Q1 | Reviewed all debt maturities | Nothing inside 24 months
- Q2 | Exited two cyclical positions | Proceeds held in short bills
- Q4 | Added to software holdings | Averaged in over ten weeks
:::

:::key Our one rule
If we cannot explain why a business will earn more in five years, we do not own it.
:::
